claim: Seipin is an ER protein implicated in LD biology.
source: Using Drosophila and human cells, we show here that seipin, an ER protein implicated in LD biology, mediates a discrete step in LD formation—the conversion of small, nascent LDs to larger, mature LDs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about seipin's localization and general role.

claim: Seipin mediates the conversion of small, nascent LDs to larger, mature LDs.
source: Using Drosophila and human cells, we show here that seipin, an ER protein implicated in LD biology, mediates a discrete step in LD formation—the conversion of small, nascent LDs to larger, mature LDs.
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Seipin forms discrete and dynamic foci in the ER.
source: Seipin forms discrete and dynamic foci in the ER that interact with nascent LDs to enable their growth.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data showing seipin localization patterns.

claim: Seipin foci interact with nascent LDs to enable their growth.
source: Seipin forms discrete and dynamic foci in the ER that interact with nascent LDs to enable their growth.
evidence: This is demonstrated through live-cell imaging experiments showing seipin-LD interactions.

claim: In the absence of seipin, numerous small, nascent LDs accumulate near the ER.
source: In the absence of seipin, numerous small, nascent LDs accumulate near the ER and most often fail to grow.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing accumulation of small LDs in seipin-deficient cells.

claim: Nascent LDs in seipin-deficient cells most often fail to grow.
source: In the absence of seipin, numerous small, nascent LDs accumulate near the ER and most often fail to grow.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course imaging and size measurements of LDs.

claim: LDs that do grow in seipin deficiency prematurely acquire lipid synthesis enzymes.
source: Those that do grow prematurely acquire lipid synthesis enzymes and undergo expansion, eventually leading to the giant LDs characteristic of seipin deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing early GPAT4 targeting to LDs in seipin-deficient cells.

claim: LDs that grow in seipin deficiency undergo expansion, eventually leading to giant LDs.
source: Those that do grow prematurely acquire lipid synthesis enzymes and undergo expansion, eventually leading to the giant LDs characteristic of seipin deficiency.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course imaging showing formation of giant LDs in seipin-deficient cells.

claim: Giant LDs are characteristic of seipin deficiency.
source: Those that do grow prematurely acquire lipid synthesis enzymes and undergo expansion, eventually leading to the giant LDs characteristic of seipin deficiency.
evidence: This is a well-established phenotype observed in multiple model systems and cited in the literature.

claim: Seipin likely acts at ER-LD contact sites to enable lipid transfer to nascent LDs.
source: Our studies identify a discrete step of LD formation, namely the conversion of nascent LDs to mature LDs, and define a molecular role for seipin in this process, most likely by acting at ER-LD contact sites to enable lipid transfer to nascent LDs.
evidence: This is inferred from electron tomography and live-cell imaging data showing seipin localization and LD-ER contacts.

claim: Lipid droplets act as reservoirs to store neutral lipids for metabolic energy and cell membrane components.
source: Lipid droplets (LDs) are cellular organelles that act as reservoirs to store neutral lipids for metabolic energy and cell membrane components (for reviews, see Gross and Silver, 2014; Hashemi and Goodman, 2015; Pol et al., 2014; Walther and Farese, 2012; Welte, 2015; Wilfling et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple review citations.

claim: The mechanism underlying the initial formation of LDs is mostly unknown.
source: Although most eukaryotic cells make LDs, the mechanism underlying the initial formation of LDs is mostly unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of publication.

claim: Excess storage of neutral lipids in LDs underlies many common metabolic diseases, such as obesity.
source: Excess storage of neutral lipids, such as triacylglycerols (TGs) and sterol esters, in LDs underlies many common metabolic diseases, such as obesity.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the relationship between lipid storage and disease.

claim: LD formation corresponds to establishing an oil-in-water emulsion.
source: In essence, LD formation corresponds to establishing an oil-in-water emulsion (Thiam et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is a biophysical characterization supported by a citation.

claim: Enzymes utilize fatty acids and glycerolipids to synthesize neutral lipids, such as TGs, in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: In the initial step, enzymes utilize fatty acids and glycerolipids to synthesize neutral lipids, such as TGs, in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about lipid synthesis pathways.

claim: TGs are packaged into nascent LDs that grow and are thought to bud from the ER to form initial LDs.
source: TGs are subsequently packaged into nascent LDs that grow and are thought to bud from the ER to form initial LDs (iLDs).
evidence: This describes the current model of LD formation based on existing literature.

claim: A subset of mature iLDs is converted to expanding LDs when specific TG synthesis enzymes migrate from the ER to LDs via membrane bridges.
source: A subset of the mature iLDs is converted to expanding LDs (eLDs) when specific TG synthesis enzymes [e.g., glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT4) and acyl CoA:diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 2 (DGAT2)] migrate from the ER to LDs via membrane bridges (Wilfling et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Targeting of GPAT4 to LDs and formation of membrane bridges depends on the Arf1/COP-I proteins.
source: Targeting of GPAT4 to LDs and formation of these bridges depends on the Arf1/COP-I proteins (Wilfling et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CCT1 binds to phosphatidylcholine-poor surfaces of eLDs, where it becomes activated and catalyzes the synthesis of PC to coat eLD surfaces.
source: Another enzyme, CTP:phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase 1 (CCT1), binds to phosphatidylcholine (PC)-poor surfaces of eLDs, where it becomes activated and catalyzes the synthesis of PC to coat eLD surfaces (Krahmer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The seipin gene was initially identified by mutations in rare but severe forms of congenital generalized lipodystrophy.
source: The seipin gene was initially identified by mutations in rare but severe forms of congenital generalized lipodystrophy (Magré et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a historical fact about the discovery of seipin, supported by a citation.

claim: In yeast lacking seipin homologue Fld1, cells have many small LDs or a few 'supersized' or giant LDs, depending on growth conditions.
source: Subsequently, LD morphology screens in Saccharomyces cerevisiae showed that the seipin homologue Fld1 is required for normal LDs; in its absence, cells have many small LDs or a few 'supersized' or giant LDs, depending on growth conditions (Fei et al., 2008; Szymanski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in yeast.

claim: Seipin is an integral membrane protein with two transmembrane domains and a large, evolutionarily conserved ER luminal loop.
source: Seipin is an integral membrane protein with two transmembrane domains and a large, evolutionarily conserved ER luminal loop (Agarwal and Garg, 2004; Lundin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a structural characterization supported by citations.

claim: Seipin forms oligomers.
source: Seipin forms oligomers (Binns et al., 2010; Sim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: In yeast, seipin localizes to ER-LD contact regions.
source: In yeast, seipin localizes to ER-LD contact regions (Grippa et al., 2015; Szymanski et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2014), and yeast cells lacking seipin have abnormal LD formation (Cartwright et al., 2015; Grippa et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014), suggesting a role for seipin in organizing this process.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to yeast studies.

claim: Yeast cells lacking seipin have abnormal LD formation.
source: In yeast, seipin localizes to ER-LD contact regions (Grippa et al., 2015; Szymanski et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2014), and yeast cells lacking seipin have abnormal LD formation (Cartwright et al., 2015; Grippa et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014), suggesting a role for seipin in organizing this process.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to yeast studies.

claim: Depletion of seipin from Drosophila S2 cells by RNAi led to formation of giant LDs after prolonged oleic acid treatment.
source: As reported (Fei et al., 2011b, 2008; Szymanski et al., 2007; Tian et al., 2011), we showed that depletion of seipin from Drosophila S2 cells by RNAi (~80% knockdown efficiency, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) led to formation of giant LDs after prolonged oleic acid treatment to induce LD formation (Figure 1A, 24 hr).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citations to previous reports.

claim: Within 1 hr of adding oleic acid to cells, LDs in seipin-depleted cells were larger than those in control cells.
source: Within 1 hr of adding oleic acid to cells, LDs in seipin-depleted cells were larger than those in control cells, although almost all LDs were less than 2 μm in diameter (Figure 1A and B, top).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Giant LDs (diameter ≥ 2 μm) first appeared in seipin knockdown cells ~5 hr after adding oleic acid.
source: Giant LDs (diameter ≥ 2 μm) first appeared in seipin knockdown cells ~5 hr after adding oleic acid and were more prevalent after 8 hr.
evidence: This is based on time-course microscopy data.

claim: Giant LDs were rare in control cells.
source: In contrast, giant LDs were rare in control cells.
evidence: This is based on microscopy data comparing control and seipin-depleted cells.

claim: Seipin-depleted cells had fewer LDs than control cells, particularly at later times.
source: Seipin-depleted cells also had fewer LDs than control cells, particularly at later times (Figure 1B, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The total areas with BODIPY-stained LD signal in optical sections of seipin-depleted cells and control cells at late time points were similar.
source: Since the total areas with BODIPY-stained LD signal in optical sections of seipin-depleted cells and control cells at late time points were similar, the LDs likely coalesced in seipin-deficient cells.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of microscopy data.

claim: LDs likely coalesced in seipin-deficient cells.
source: Since the total areas with BODIPY-stained LD signal in optical sections of seipin-depleted cells and control cells at late time points were similar, the LDs likely coalesced in seipin-deficient cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that total LD area is similar but LD number is reduced.

claim: Rates of accumulation of TG, PC, and PE were similar in control and seipin knockdown cells both in cell homogenates and microsomes.
source: Rates of accumulation of TG, PC, and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) were similar in control and seipin knockdown cells both in cell homogenates (Figure 1C) and microsomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating similar rates of glycerolipid synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by metabolic labeling experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Steady-state levels and synthesis rates of lipids in seipin-depleted cells showed no differences by high-resolution shotgun lipidomics at 3 hr after adding [13C5]-oleic acid.
source: Steady-state levels and synthesis rates of lipids in seipin-depleted cells showed no differences by high-resolution shotgun lipidomics (Almeida et al., 2015; Ejsing et al., 2009) at 3 hr after adding [13C5]-oleic acid (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LC-MS/MS lipidomics did not show evidence of altered lipid metabolism between control and seipin knockout cells without oleic acid.
source: LC-MS/MS lipidomics did not show evidence of altered lipid metabolism (for instance, levels of PC, PE or TG) between control and seipin knockout cells without oleic acid (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: No increase in cellular PA levels was found in seipin-deficient cells.
source: Although others reported an accumulation of phosphatidic acid (PA) in seipin-deficient yeast (Fei et al., 2011b, 2011c; Sim et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2011; Wolinski et al., 2015), we found no increase in cellular PA levels (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data and contrasts with previous reports in yeast.

claim: Expression of GFP-PASS probe did not accumulate at any specific site in cells during LD formation.
source: Additionally, expression of a probe, GFP-PASS (Lu et al., 2016), that senses the accumulation of PA and possibly other anionic phospholipids (Horchani et al., 2014) did not accumulate at any specific site in cells during LD formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The ER morphology appeared normal in seipin-depleted cells.
source: However, the ER morphology appeared normal in seipin-depleted cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and we did not find evidence of altered ER lipid composition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No evidence of altered ER lipid composition was found in seipin-depleted cells.
source: However, the ER morphology appeared normal in seipin-depleted cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and we did not find evidence of altered ER lipid composition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data from microsomal fractions.

claim: The abnormal LD phenotype found in seipin depletion does not likely result from defects in whole-cell or global ER lipid metabolism.
source: Thus, the abnormal LD phenotype found in seipin depletion does not likely result from defects in whole-cell or global ER lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of changes in lipid metabolism measurements.

claim: LiveDrop contains the membrane hairpin domain (amino acids 160–216) of the glycerolipid synthesis enzyme GPAT4 fused to a fluorescent protein.
source: We therefore developed a probe, which we named LiveDrop, that contains the membrane hairpin domain (amino acids 160–216) of the glycerolipid synthesis enzyme GPAT4 fused to a fluorescent protein (mCherry or eGFP) (Wilfling et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the design of the LiveDrop probe.

claim: LiveDrop localizes from the ER to all newly synthesized LDs upon their formation.
source: Although full-length GPAT4 normally localizes only to eLDs (Wilfling et al., 2013), LiveDrop localizes from the ER to all newly synthesized LDs upon their formation (Figure 2A,C, control) and identifies TG collections before BODIPY (as seen in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: LiveDrop identifies TG collections before BODIPY.
source: Although full-length GPAT4 normally localizes only to eLDs (Wilfling et al., 2013), LiveDrop localizes from the ER to all newly synthesized LDs upon their formation (Figure 2A,C, control) and identifies TG collections before BODIPY (as seen in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course imaging showing LiveDrop signal before BODIPY signal.

claim: LiveDrop localization to foci that become LDs depends on TG synthesis.
source: LiveDrop localization to foci that become LDs depends on TG synthesis (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), and in in vitro experiments using adhesive emulsion (Thiam et al., 2012), we found that LiveDrop partitions preferentially into monolayers over bilayer membranes compared with a control protein Arf1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experiments with TG synthesis inhibitors shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: LiveDrop partitions preferentially into monolayers over bilayer membranes compared with a control protein Arf1.
source: LiveDrop localization to foci that become LDs depends on TG synthesis (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), and in in vitro experiments using adhesive emulsion (Thiam et al., 2012), we found that LiveDrop partitions preferentially into monolayers over bilayer membranes compared with a control protein Arf1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro adhesive emulsion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In control cells, LiveDrop rapidly accumulated in small puncta that grew larger within minutes and subsequently became detectable with BODIPY.
source: In control cells, when LD formation was induced by oleic acid, LiveDrop, which was initially diffuse within the ER, rapidly accumulated in small puncta that grew larger within minutes and subsequently became detectable with BODIPY (Figure 2A,B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in multiple figures and videos.

claim: The ER of seipin-deficient cells had large numbers (up to an average of 60 per cell) of small LiveDrop puncta that mostly did not grow large enough to stain with BODIPY.
source: In contrast, the ER of seipin-deficient cells had large numbers (up to an average of 60 per cell, Figure 2B) of small LiveDrop puncta that mostly did not grow large enough to stain with BODIPY (Figure 2A,B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and Videos 1, 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2B and imaging data.

claim: LiveDrop puncta in seipin-deficient cells stayed small and highly mobile (0.23 ± 0.06 μm/s) at the ER.
source: Instead, they stayed small and highly mobile (0.23 ± 0.06 μm/s) at the ER (Figure 2D,E and Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by tracking analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: BODIPY-stained LDs formed in control cells were relatively static (0.07 ± 0.02 μm/s), compared with LiveDrop puncta in seipin-depleted cells.
source: BODIPY-stained LDs formed in control cells were relatively static (0.07 ± 0.02 μm/s), compared with LiveDrop puncta in seipin-depleted cells (Figure 2D,E and Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by tracking analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Inhibition of TG synthesis abolished the LiveDrop puncta in seipin-knockdown cells.
source: These treatments abolished the LiveDrop puncta, indicating that they depend on TG synthesis and are likely very small TG collections associated with the ER.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with TG synthesis inhibitors shown in Figure 2F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: LiveDrop puncta in seipin-knockdown cells are likely very small TG collections associated with the ER.
source: These treatments abolished the LiveDrop puncta, indicating that they depend on TG synthesis and are likely very small TG collections associated with the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the dependence on TG synthesis and localization patterns.

claim: SUM159 seipin knockout cells showed numerous, BODIPY-negative LiveDrop puncta upon oleate treatment.
source: In each mammalian seipin-defective cell line, LiveDrop formed numerous, BODIPY-negative puncta upon oleate treatment (Figure 3A,B, and Videos 5, 6), recapitulating the findings from seipin knockdown S2 cells.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Primary fibroblasts from patients with congenital generalized lipodystrophy type 2 showed numerous, BODIPY-negative LiveDrop puncta upon oleate treatment.
source: In each mammalian seipin-defective cell line, LiveDrop formed numerous, BODIPY-negative puncta upon oleate treatment (Figure 3A,B, and Videos 5, 6), recapitulating the findings from seipin knockdown S2 cells.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After prolonged oleic acid treatment (24 hr), giant LDs formed in each seipin deficiency model.
source: After prolonged oleic acid treatment (24 hr), giant LDs formed in each seipin deficiency model.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: In mammalian cells, unlike Drosophila S2 cells, there were very few giant LDs and more numerous small puncta that were weakly detected by BODIPY staining after prolonged oleic acid treatment.
source: However, unlike Drosophila S2 cells, there were very few giant LDs and more numerous small puncta that were weakly detected by BODIPY staining (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: ER morphology seemed normal in seipin-knockout cells.
source: Of note, ER morphology seemed normal in seipin-knockout cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and there were no changes in ER lipid composition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or in the activity of ER stress pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There were no changes in ER lipid composition in seipin-knockout cells.
source: Of note, ER morphology seemed normal in seipin-knockout cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and there were no changes in ER lipid composition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or in the activity of ER stress pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There were no changes in the activity of ER stress pathways in seipin-knockout cells.
source: Of note, ER morphology seemed normal in seipin-knockout cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and there were no changes in ER lipid composition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or in the activity of ER stress pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by ER stress marker analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Expression of full-length Drosophila seipin dramatically reduced the numbers of LiveDrop puncta in most knockdown cells.
source: When full-length Drosophila seipin was expressed in the knockdown cells, the numbers of LiveDrop puncta were dramatically reduced in most cells.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Tagging seipin with a fluorescent protein localized to the N- or C-terminus resulted in similar rescue efficiency 30 min after oleate loading.
source: Tagging with a fluorescent protein localized to the N- or C-terminus resulted in similar rescue efficiency 30 min after oleate loading (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Deletion of the N- or C-terminal cytosolic domain or both did not affect the rescue efficiency of seipin overexpression.
source: Deletion of the N- or C-terminal cytosolic domain or both did not affect the rescue efficiency of seipin overexpression.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments with truncation mutants shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Expression of the N- or C-terminus alone did not rescue the phenotype.
source: In contrast, expression of the N- or C-terminus alone did not rescue the phenotype (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The evolutionarily conserved regions of seipin (i.e., the ER luminal domain and transmembrane domains) are required for seipin's function in organizing iLD formation.
source: These results suggest that the evolutionarily conserved regions of seipin (i.e., the ER luminal domain and transmembrane domains) are required for seipin's function in organizing iLD formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with truncation mutants.

claim: Expression of human seipin in seipin-depleted Drosophila S2 cells completely abolished abnormal LiveDrop puncta accumulation.
source: In agreement with evolutionary conservation of seipin's function, expression of human seipin in seipin-depleted Drosophila S2 cells completely abolished abnormal LiveDrop puncta accumulation, and mature iLDs formed normally in all transfected cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Wildtype cells contained numerous mature iLDs ranging in diameter between 200–500 nm, with an average of ~300 nm, after 60 min of oleate treatment.
source: Consistent with images obtained by live cell imaging, wildtype cells contained numerous mature iLDs ranging in diameter between 200–500 nm, with an average of ~300 nm, after 60 min of oleate treatment (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Seipin-deficient cells showed a large accumulation of nascent LDs of uniform size of less than 200 nm diameter, with an average of ~170 nm.
source: In contrast, seipin-deficient cells showed a large accumulation of nascent LDs of uniform size of less than 200 nm diameter, with an average of ~170 nm (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Nascent LDs in seipin-deficient cells were most often located in close proximity to the ER.
source: These nascent LDs were most often located in close proximity to the ER.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy observations.

claim: The nascent LDs in seipin-deficient cells were always in close proximity to the ER and their surface monolayer was separated from the ER membrane.
source: We found that the nascent LDs in seipin-deficient cells were always in close proximity to the ER and that their surface monolayer was separated from the ER membrane (Figure 5C,D and Videos 7, 8, 9 and 10).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Ribosomes appeared to be absent from the space between the nascent LDs and the ER.
source: Modeling of the tomograms indicated that ribosomes appeared to be absent from the space between the nascent LDs and the ER and that this space sometimes had electron density Figure 5D and Video 11.
evidence: This is based on modeling of electron tomography data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The LiveDrop puncta represent nascent LDs that are separate from, but in close contact with the ER, and that fail to grow to the size of normal, mature iLDs.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the LiveDrop puncta represent nascent LDs that are separate from, but in close contact with the ER, and that fail to grow to the size of normal, mature iLDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of live-cell imaging and electron tomography data.

claim: Without oleic acid, GFP-seipin formed distinct foci in cells that overlapped with an ER marker.
source: Without oleic acid, GFP-seipin formed distinct foci in cells that overlapped with an ER marker (ss-BFP-KDEL; (Dayel et al., 1999) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Seipin foci did not localize to any specific domain of the ER (e.g., tubules, sheets, tips).
source: These foci did not localize to any specific domain of the ER (e.g., tubules, sheets, tips) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) or three-way junctions marked by lunapark (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and they moved rapidly along the ER (1.06 ± 0.22 μm/s; Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Video 12).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Seipin foci moved rapidly along the ER (1.06 ± 0.22 μm/s).
source: These foci did not localize to any specific domain of the ER (e.g., tubules, sheets, tips) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) or three-way junctions marked by lunapark (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and they moved rapidly along the ER (1.06 ± 0.22 μm/s; Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Video 12).
evidence: This is supported by tracking analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: By 5 min after adding oleic acid, many LiveDrop puncta and seipin foci became co-localized.
source: Upon adding oleic acid to form LDs, LiveDrop puncta initially were distinct from GFP-seipin foci. However, by 5 min, many LiveDrop puncta and seipin foci became co-localized.
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data.

claim: Once LiveDrop puncta and seipin foci became co-localized, the individual LiveDrop punctum was stabilized and began to grow in volume.
source: Once this occurred, the individual LiveDrop punctum was stabilized and began to grow in volume (Figure 3C and Video 13).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6C and Video 13.

claim: Seipin foci associated with nascent LDs became relatively immobile (0.52 ± 0.09 μm/s).
source: Consistent with this model, seipin foci associated with nascent LDs became relatively immobile (0.52 ± 0.09 μm/s), whereas those not associated with nascent LDs were highly dynamic (0.89 ± 0.19 μm/s; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by tracking analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Seipin foci not associated with nascent LDs were highly dynamic (0.89 ± 0.19 μm/s).
source: Consistent with this model, seipin foci associated with nascent LDs became relatively immobile (0.52 ± 0.09 μm/s), whereas those not associated with nascent LDs were highly dynamic (0.89 ± 0.19 μm/s; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by tracking analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: At 3 hr or later after adding oleic acid, almost every LD was associated with at least one seipin focus.
source: At 3 hr or later after adding oleic acid, almost every LD was associated with at least one seipin focus (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There were many more seipin foci than LDs, and many seipin foci did not localize to LDs.
source: However, there were many more seipin foci than LDs, and many seipin foci did not localize to LDs.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations.

claim: GPAT4 targets to LDs as early as 10 min after LD formation is induced by oleic acid in seipin-depleted cells.
source: Immunofluorescence of endogenous GPAT4 in seipin-depleted cells showed that GPAT4 targets to LDs as early as 10 min after LD formation is induced by oleic acid.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In control cells, GPAT4 localizes to LDs much later (not until 1 hr after induction of LDs).
source: In control cells, GPAT4 localizes to LDs much later (Figure 7A) (not until 1 hr after induction of LDs, not shown).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data.

claim: At 20 min after adding oleic acid, 18% of LDs in seipin knockdown cells were marked by GPAT4, but only 1–2% in control cells were GPAT4-positive.
source: At 20 min after adding oleic acid, 18% of LDs in seipin knockdown cells were marked by GPAT4, but only 1–2% in control cells were GPAT4-positive (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: After prolonged oleic acid treatment (8 hr), 8% of LDs in wild-type cells were GPAT4-positive, compared with 72% in seipin-depleted cells.
source: After prolonged oleic acid treatment (8 hr), 8% of LDs in wild-type cells were GPAT4-positive, compared with 72% in seipin-depleted cells (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Most of the GPAT4 pool was localized to LDs in seipin-depleted cells, and little remained in the ER.
source: In fact, most of the GPAT4 pool was localized to LDs in seipin-depleted cells, and little remained in the ER (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Accumulation of nascent iLDs in seipin deficiency caused aberrant GPAT4 targeting to LDs, thereby initiating localized TG synthesis and LD expansion prematurely.
source: This observation suggests that accumulation of nascent iLDs in seipin deficiency caused aberrant GPAT4 targeting to LDs, thereby initiating localized TG synthesis and LD expansion prematurely.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of early GPAT4 targeting in seipin-deficient cells.

claim: Knockdown of enzymes of the LD expansion pathway abolished the giant LDs (diameter > 2.5 μm) of seipin deficiency.
source: Knockdown of enzymes of the LD expansion pathway abolished the giant LDs (diameter > 2.5 μm) of seipin deficiency, but knockdown of enzymes of the non-LD pathway did not affect LD size in seipin knockdown cells (Figure 7D, yellow box).
evidence: This is supported by double knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Knockdown of enzymes of the non-LD pathway did not affect LD size in seipin knockdown cells.
source: Knockdown of enzymes of the LD expansion pathway abolished the giant LDs (diameter > 2.5 μm) of seipin deficiency, but knockdown of enzymes of the non-LD pathway did not affect LD size in seipin knockdown cells (Figure 7D, yellow box).
evidence: This is supported by double knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Incorporation of label into phospholipids (PC and PE) specifically on LDs was decreased in seipin-depleted cells at 5–8 hr after adding oleic acid to cells.
source: However, incorporation of label into phospholipids (PC and PE) specifically on LDs was decreased in seipin-depleted cells at 5–8 hr after adding oleic acid to cells, indicating a relative deficiency of phospholipids in LDs of seipin-depleted cells at these late times.
evidence: This is supported by metabolic labeling experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The ratio of surface phospholipids to TG (i.e., PC/TG or PE/TG) decreased markedly at 5-8 hr after adding oleic acid in seipin-depleted cells.
source: As a consequence, the ratio of surface phospholipids to TG (i.e., PC/TG or PE/TG) decreased markedly at this time (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic labeling data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Phospholipid deficiency on LDs results in their coalescence to form giant LDs.
source: This observation is consistent with the time course of LD formation (Figure 1A), with giant LDs forming 5–8 hr after adding oleic acid, and suggests phospholipid deficiency on LDs results in their coalescence to form giant LDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between phospholipid deficiency and giant LD formation.

claim: Seipin-depleted cells exhibited earlier and markedly increased CCT1 targeting to LDs, compared with control cells.
source: Indeed, seipin-depleted cells exhibited earlier and markedly increased CCT1 targeting to LDs, compared with control cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: When seipin-deficient cells were treated with PC liposomes or choline supplementation, no giant LDs (diameter > 2.5 μm) in seipin deficiency were formed.
source: Further, when seipin-deficient cells were treated with PC liposomes or choline supplementation, no giant LDs (diameter > 2.5 μm) in seipin deficiency were formed (Figure 8C, yellow box).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claim: CCT1 depletion aggravated the seipin knockdown phenotype.
source: As expected, CCT1 depletion aggravated, and ECT depletion abolished, the seipin knockdown phenotype (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by double knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: ECT depletion abolished the seipin knockdown phenotype.
source: As expected, CCT1 depletion aggravated, and ECT depletion abolished, the seipin knockdown phenotype (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by double knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Faster LD expansion in seipin-depleted cells leads to more eLDs with transient PC deficiency, and this likely leads to LD coalescence to form giant LDs.
source: These data suggest that faster LD expansion in seipin-depleted cells leads to more eLDs with transient PC deficiency, and this likely leads to LD coalescence to form giant LDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of phospholipid deficiency data and rescue experiments.

claim: Seipin acts at a distinct step of LD biogenesis, after nascent LDs form during iLD formation.
source: Here, we investigated seipin function in LD formation in Drosophila and mammalian cells. We found that seipin acts at a distinct step of LD biogenesis, after nascent LDs form during iLD formation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Seipin localizes to ER-LD contact sites and enables nascent LDs to acquire more lipids from the ER and grow to form mature iLDs.
source: Our data suggest that seipin localizes to ER-LD contact sites and enables nascent LDs to acquire more lipids from the ER and grow to form mature iLDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of live-cell imaging and electron tomography data.

claim: Without seipin, the process of nascent LD growth appears to be blocked, resulting in massive accumulation of small nascent LDs.
source: Without seipin, this process appears to be blocked, resulting in massive accumulation of small nascent LDs.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and electron microscopy data showing accumulation of small LDs.

claim: The few LDs that do grow in seipin deficiency exhibit aberrant targeting of lipid synthesis enzymes, such as GPAT4, involved in forming eLDs.
source: The few LDs that do grow exhibit aberrant targeting of lipid synthesis enzymes, such as GPAT4, involved in forming eLDs.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing early GPAT4 targeting.

claim: Aberrant targeting of lipid synthesis enzymes likely explains the giant LD phenotype characteristically found in seipin-deficient cells.
source: The latter process likely explains the giant LD phenotype characteristically found in seipin-deficient cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of GPAT4 targeting data and rescue experiments.

claim: Seipin functions downstream of initial lens formation and TG budding, at a more distal step in the maturation of nascent LDs.
source: However, with seipin depletion, progression through this step is blocked, resulting in the apparent accumulation of large numbers of intermediates (small, nascent LDs), found in our studies by electron tomography, that fail to mature. These findings indicate that seipin functions downstream of initial lens formation and TG budding, at a more distal step in the maturation of nascent LDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nascent LDs form but fail to grow in seipin deficiency.

claim: Seipin oligomers form a toroid-structure comprising approximately 8–12 seipin proteins.
source: These studies indicated that purified seipin forms oligomers in a toroid-structure comprising approximately 8–12 seipin proteins (Binns et al., 2010; Cartwright and Goodman, 2012; Sim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: From live-cell imaging, the seipin foci include considerably more molecular units in cells than the 8-12 proteins in purified oligomers.
source: However, from live-cell imaging, we estimate that the seipin foci include considerably more molecular units in cells (not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from live-cell imaging observations.

claim: Seipin oligomers anchored in the ER possibly mediate specific contacts with the surface monolayer of nascent LDs and enable the transfer of lipids to the nascent LDs, allowing them to grow.
source: Possibly seipin oligomers anchored in the ER mediate specific contacts with the surface monolayer of nascent LDs and enable the transfer of lipids (such as TG) to the nascent LDs, allowing them to grow (see model, Figure 9).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Seipin's function in converting nascent LDs to mature iLDs is likely its ancient, primary function.
source: Our findings suggest that seipin's function in converting nascent LDs to mature iLDs is likely its ancient, primary function.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary conservation of the phenotype and rescue by human seipin.

claim: Seipin deficiency resulted in similar phenotypes of larger numbers of LiveDrop-positive foci in cells from flies, human mammary carcinoma cells, and human fibroblasts from seipin-deficient subjects.
source: In support of this, seipin deficiency resulted in similar phenotypes of larger numbers of LiveDrop-positive foci in cells from flies, human mammary carcinoma cells, and human fibroblasts from seipin-deficient subjects.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from multiple cell types.

claim: The overexpressed N-terminus of Drosophila seipin localized to LDs.
source: We found that the overexpressed N-terminus of Drosophila seipin localized to LDs (Figure 4A), suggesting that this part of the protein, though not required for formation, may aid in interaction with LDs.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In yeast, the N-terminus of seipin was found to be functionally important with respect to the timing of LD formation.
source: In yeast, the N-terminus was found to be functionally important with respect to the timing of LD formation (Cartwright et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study in yeast.

claim: In the absence of seipin, large numbers of nascent iLDs accumulate, and some of these LDs aberrantly entered the LD expansion pathway.
source: In the absence of seipin, we found that large numbers of nascent iLDs accumulate, and some of these LDs aberrantly entered the LD expansion pathway.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing accumulation of small LDs and early GPAT4 targeting.

claim: Lipid synthesis enzymes, such as GPAT4 and CCT1, that are normally found only on late-forming eLDs were aberrantly targeted to iLDs at early time points in seipin-deficient cells.
source: In support of this, lipid synthesis enzymes, such as GPAT4 and CCT1, that are normally found only on late-forming eLDs were aberrantly targeted to iLDs at early time points, and this mislocalization of eLD proteins to iLDs was crucial for the development of the giant LD phenotype at later time points.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing early enzyme targeting.

claim: Mislocalization of eLD proteins to iLDs was crucial for the development of the giant LD phenotype at later time points.
source: In support of this, lipid synthesis enzymes, such as GPAT4 and CCT1, that are normally found only on late-forming eLDs were aberrantly targeted to iLDs at early time points, and this mislocalization of eLD proteins to iLDs was crucial for the development of the giant LD phenotype at later time points.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments showing that knockdown of LD expansion enzymes prevents giant LD formation.

claim: Similar abnormal protein targeting to LDs was recently found in yeast lacking seipin orthologues.
source: Similar abnormal protein targeting to LDs was recently found in yeast lacking seipin orthologues (Grippa et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent yeast studies.

claim: Cells lacking seipin can still form LDs, but these LDs have irregular size and abnormal lipid and protein composition.
source: Cells lacking seipin can still form LDs, but these LDs have irregular size and abnormal lipid and protein composition, which likely leads to cellular dysfunction with respect to storing and reclaiming lipids for cellular needs.
evidence: This is supported by the various measurements of LD size, lipid composition, and protein localization.

claim: Seipin deficiency in humans leads to severe generalized lipodystrophy, with a near absence of adipose mass.
source: In support of this notion, seipin deficiency in humans leads to severe generalized lipodystrophy, with a near absence of adipose mass (Magré et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Seipin likely works in concert with other proteins that mediate ER-LD contact to enable the growth of nascent LDs.
source: Our findings also suggest that seipin likely works in concert with other proteins that mediate ER-LD contact to enable the growth of nascent LDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ER-LD contacts persist in seipin deficiency.
